text:
Recent work supports separating preference timescales. [MSMT-LSI (2024)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s44196-024-00460-5) uses separate long/short self-attention networks with temporal embeddings. [Hierarchical long/short preference modeling (2025)](https://journal.hep.com.cn/fcs/EN/10.1007/s11704-025-41181-y) represents older history with multiple interest vectors, matches these against current short-term intent, and fuses them through time encoding. The useful principle: retrieve relevant older preferences rather than average all history into one broad vector.

Repetition and noise deserve separate treatment. [LSIDN (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.14743) gives long/short branches different encoders and denoising strategies. [GDA-REIM (2026)](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0893608026001838) combines differential attention with repetition–exploration scoring and an intent-discrimination loss. Its historical-item pointer is relevant when repeat consumption is allowed; for unseen-item recommendations, recurring interests should instead guide scores toward related unseen items. [Dual-Interest Multi-Granular SSM (2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21548) separates stable-history aggregation from local intent, using interaction gaps to modulate short-term state evolution.

Practical synthesis, rather than a directly validated architecture: retain SASRec for recent intent; add a small bank of pooled historical interests and a recurrence-sensitive branch using learned item similarities. Fuse branch scores with a gate conditioned on recent features, elapsed gaps, and history length. Compare fixed mixing against learned gating, then add timestamp decay and multiple historical vectors separately. This offers a lightweight way to test whether stale affinities are suppressing current intent; the cited results do not establish gains on the pinned RecHarness evaluation.
